'''Eric Steven Lander''' (born February 3, 1957) is an American mathematician and geneticist  who is a professor of biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), and a professor of systems biology at [[Harvard Medical School]].

Lander received a MacArthur Fellowship.  He founded the [[WICGR|Whitehead Institute Center for Genome Research]], was a principal leader of the [[Human Genome Project]], and was the founding director of the [[Broad Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-11-23 |title=Eric S. Lander |url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/bios/eric-s-lander |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=Broad Institute |language=en}}</ref>  He was [[Science Advisor to the President]] for Presidents Obama and Biden.

==Early life and education==
Lander was born in [[Brooklyn]], New York City,<ref>{{cite web |title= Eric S. Lander, Ph.D. Career Highlights |url = http://www.hhmi.org/biointeractive/genomics/lander_career.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101230082800/http://www.hhmi.org/biointeractive/genomics/lander_career.html |date=December 30, 2010 | archive-date= December 30, 2010 | publisher = Howard Hughes Medical Institute | access-date = May 26, 2020 }}</ref> to [[American Jews|Jewish]] parents,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://library.cshl.edu/oralhistory/interview/james-d-watson/personality-influence/spirituality-science/ |title=Oral History &#124; James D. Watson &#124; Personality & Influence &#124; Eric Lander on Spirituality & Science |publisher=Library.cshl.edu |date=June 2, 2003 |access-date=February 23, 2015}}</ref> the son of Rhoda G. Lander, a social studies teacher, and Harold Lander, an attorney.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Corry |first1=John |title=About New York |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/03/25/archives/about-new-york-smart-kid-on-the-block.html |access-date=January 16, 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 25, 1974}}</ref> He was captain of the math team at [[Stuyvesant High School]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Olson|first=Steve|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ctkwbaws7gC&q=eric+lander+captain+of+math+team&pg=PA2|title=Count Down: Six Kids Vie for Glory at the World's Toughest Math Competition|publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company|year=2005|isbn=978-0-618-56212-1|location=Boston, New York|page=2}}</ref> graduating in 1974 as valedictorian and an [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] Silver Medalist for the U.S.<ref name="time" /> At age 17, he wrote a paper on [[quasiperfect number]]s, for which he won the 1974 [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref name=time>{{cite magazine |last1=Elmer-DeWitt |first1=Philip |title=The 2004 Time 100: Scientists & Thinkers: Eric Lander |url=https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,1970858_1970909_1971674,00.html |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=April 26, 2004 |access-date=February 25, 2019 |ref=time}}</ref>

After graduating from [[Stuyvesant High School]] as valedictorian in 1974, Lander graduated from [[Princeton University]] in 1978 as valedictorian and with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in mathematics.<ref name="time" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Eric S. Lander|url=https://biology.mit.edu/profile/eric-s-lander/|access-date=June 4, 2021|website=MIT Department of Biology}}</ref> He completed his senior thesis, "On the structure of projective modules", under [[John Coleman Moore]]'s supervision.<ref name="bach">{{cite thesis | degree=Bachelor| first=Eric | last=Lander |title=On the structure of projective modules |publisher= Princeton University | url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/3705900 | access-date=February 21, 2018}}</ref> He then moved to the [[University of Oxford]] where he was a [[Rhodes Scholar]] and student of [[Wolfson College, Oxford]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Wolfson Alumnus Eric Lander named top scientific adviser by Joe Biden {{!}} Wolfson College, Oxford|url=https://www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk/news/wolfson-alumnus-eric-lander-named-top-scientific-adviser-joe-biden|access-date=June 4, 2021|website=www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk|archive-date=July 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210714153116/https://www.wolfson.ox.ac.uk/news/wolfson-alumnus-eric-lander-named-top-scientific-adviser-joe-biden|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree by the [[University of Oxford]] in 1980 with a thesis on algebraic [[coding theory]] and [[Symmetric design|symmetric block design]]s supervised by [[Peter Cameron (mathematician)|Peter Cameron]].<ref name="dphil">{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|first=Eric Steven|last=Lander|title=Topics in algebraic coding theory|publisher=University of Oxford|date=1980|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=oxfaleph016690714|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.276073}}|oclc=59963645|website=ox.ac.uk|access-date=July 10, 2012|archive-date=January 7, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107075557/http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=oxfaleph016690714}}</ref>

==Career==
During his career, Lander has worked on human [[genetic variation]], human [[population history]], [[genome evolution]], [[non-coding RNA]]s, three-dimensional folding of the [[human genome]] and [[genome-wide association study|genome-wide association studies]] to discover the [[gene]]s essential for biological processes using [[CRISPR]]-based editing.

===Early mathematical career===
As a mathematician, Lander studied combinatorics and applications of [[representation theory]] to [[coding theory]]. He enjoyed mathematics but did not wish to spend his life in such a "monastic" career.<ref name="nytimes1">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/01/03/science/broad-institute-director-finds-power-in-numbers.html?pagewanted=all |title=Power in Numbers |newspaper=The New York Times |date=January 2, 2012 |access-date=February 23, 2015 |last1=Kolata |first1=Gina}}</ref> Unsure what to do next, he took a job teaching [[managerial economics]] at [[Harvard Business School]].  At the suggestion of his brother, developmental biologist [[Arthur Lander]], he started to look at neurobiology, saying at the time, "because there's a lot of information in the brain".<ref>{{cite web |title=Eric S. Lander, Ph.D. Biography and Interview |website=www.achievement.org |publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]] |url=https://achievement.org/achiever/eric-lander-ph-d/#interview}}</ref> To understand mathematical neurobiology, he felt he had to study cellular neurobiology; this, in turn, led to studying microbiology and eventually genetics. "When I finally feel I have learned genetics, I should get back to these other problems. But I'm still trying to get the genetics right", Lander said.

Lander later became acquainted with [[David Botstein]], a geneticist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Botstein was working on a way to unravel how subtle differences in complex genetic systems can become disorders such as cancer, diabetes, schizophrenia, and even obesity. The two collaborated to develop a computer algorithm to analyze the maps of genes.<ref name="nytimes1"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lander |first1=E. S. |last2=Botstein |first2=D. |year=1986 |title=Mapping complex genetic traits in humans: new methods using a complete RFLP linkage map |journal=Cold Spring Harb Symp Quant Biol |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=49–62 |doi=10.1101/sqb.1986.051.01.007 |url=https://symposium.cshlp.org/content/51/49 |access-date=June 3, 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lander |first1=E. S. |last2=Green |first2=P. |last3=Abrahamson |first3=J. |last4=Barlow |first4=A. |last5=Daly |first5=M. J. |last6=Lincoln |first6=S. E. |last7=Newberg |first7=L. A. |title=MAPMAKER: an interactive computer package for constructing primary genetic linkage maps of experimental and natural populations |journal=Genomics |date=October 1987 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=174–181 |doi=10.1016/0888-7543(87)90010-3 |pmid=3692487}}</ref> In 1986 Lander joined the [[Whitehead Institute]] and became an assistant professor at MIT. He was awarded a [[MacArthur Fellow]]ship in 1987. In 1990, he founded the Whitehead Institute/MIT Center for Genome Research (WICGR).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://historycambridge.org/innovation/Human_Genome.html |title=Human Genome Project |work=Innovation in Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge Historical Society |year=2012 |first=Katie |last=MacDonald |access-date=2025-06-21}}</ref> The WICGR became one of the world's leading centers of genome research, and under Lander's leadership made great progress in developing new methods of analyzing mammalian genomes. It also made important breakthroughs in applying this information to the study of human genetic variation and formed the basis for the foundation of the [[Broad Institute]]—a transformation Lander spearheaded.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-02-28 |title=History |url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/history |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Broad Institute |language=en}}</ref>

===Forensic science and criminal justice===

In 1989, Lander provided expert testimony in the New York criminal case ''People v. Castro''. He showed that the then-current method of interpreting DNA evidence was liable to give false positive matches, implicating innocent defendants.<ref>{{cite journal|pmc=3738447 | pmid=23950733 | doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1003692 | volume=9 | issue=8 | title=The innocence project at twenty: an interview with Barry Scheck. Interview by Jane Gitschier | year=2013 | journal=PLOS Genet. | article-number=e1003692 | last1 = Scheck | first1 = B | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.economist.com/technology-quarterly/2004/03/13/dnas-detective-story | title=DNA's detective story| newspaper=The Economist| date=March 11, 2004}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | url=http://escholarship.org/uc/item/362776cz | title=People V. Castro: Challenging the Forensic Use of DNA Evidence| journal=Journal of Scholarly Perspectives| volume=3| issue=1| year=2007| last1=Mnookin| first1=Jennifer L.}}</ref> Two of the defense attorneys in that case, [[Peter Neufeld]] and [[Barry Scheck]], went on to found the [[Innocence Project]], an organization that uses DNA analysis to exonerate wrongly convicted prisoners. Lander is a member of the Innocence Project's board of directors.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://innocenceproject.org/eric-lander-calls-for-officials-to-uphold-best-forensic-practices/|title=Eric Lander Calls For Officials to Uphold Best Forensic Practices|date=April 21, 2015|website=Innocence Project}}</ref>

===Human Genome Project===
Two main groups attempted to sequence the human genome. The first was the [[Human Genome Project]], a loosely organized, publicly funded effort that intended to publish the information it obtained freely and without restrictions. Many research groups from countries all over the world were involved in this effort. The second was undertaken by [[Celera Genomics]], which intended to [[patent]] the information obtained and charge subscriptions for use of the sequence data. Established first, the Human Genome Project moved slowly in the early phases as the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]]'s role was unclear and sequencing technology was in its infancy. Officially, the Human Genome Project had an eight-year head start before Celera entered the race, though discussions for the Human Genome Project began fourteen years before Celera announced their own project.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Human Genome Project FAQ|url=https://www.genome.gov/human-genome-project/Completion-FAQ|access-date=May 27, 2021|website=Genome.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Venter|first=J. C.|date=June 5, 1998|title=Genomics: Shotgun Sequencing of the Human Genome|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.280.5369.1540|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=280|issue=5369|pages=1540–1542|doi=10.1126/science.280.5369.1540|pmid=9644018|bibcode=1998Sci...280.1540.|s2cid=31640363|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Because the Human Genome Project was a $3 billion publicly funded venture,<ref name=":0" /> the consortia raced to enter as much of the human genome into the public domain as quickly as possible once Celera began work in 1998. This was a change of strategy for the Human Genome Project, because many scientists at the time wanted to establish a more complete copy of the genome, not simply publish the many fragments individually. Lander aggressively pressured Human Genome Project scientists to work longer and faster to publish genome fragments before Celera.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Meet Eric Lander, Biden's Pick For Science Adviser And A Polarizing Figure|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/peteraldhous/eric-lander-biden-science-adviser|access-date=May 27, 2021|website=BuzzFeed News|date=January 19, 2021 }}</ref> Lander himself is now listed on 73 patents and patent applications related to genomics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Eric S. Lander Inventions, Patents and Patent Applications – Justia Patents Search|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/eric-s-lander|access-date=May 27, 2021|website=patents.justia.com}}</ref>

In February 2001, both the Human Genome Project and Celera published drafts of the human genome in the scientific journals [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']]<ref name=":1" /> and [[Science (journal)|''Science'']],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Venter|first1=J. Craig|last2=Adams|first2=Mark D.|last3=Myers|first3=Eugene W.|last4=Li|first4=Peter W.|last5=Mural|first5=Richard J.|last6=Sutton|first6=Granger G.|last7=Smith|first7=Hamilton O.|last8=Yandell|first8=Mark|last9=Evans|first9=Cheryl A.|last10=Holt|first10=Robert A.|last11=Gocayne|first11=Jeannine D.|date=February 16, 2001|title=The Sequence of the Human Genome|journal=Science|volume=291|issue=5507|pages=1304–1351|doi=10.1126/science.1058040|pmid=11181995|bibcode=2001Sci...291.1304V|issn=0036-8075|doi-access=}}</ref> respectively. The WICGR has since sequenced the genomes of ''[[Ciona|Ciona savignyi]]'' (sea squirt),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.broad.mit.edu/annotation/ciona/ |title=Ciona savignyi Database |publisher=Broad.mit.edu |date=September 10, 2004 |access-date=February 23, 2015}}</ref> the [[pufferfish]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.broad.mit.edu/annotation/tetraodon/ |title=Tetraodon nigroviridis Database |publisher=Broad.mit.edu |date=September 10, 2004 |access-date=February 23, 2015}}</ref> the [[Hypha|filamentous]] fungus ''[[Neurospora crassa]]'',<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.broad.mit.edu/annotation/fungi/neurospora_crassa_7/index.html |title=Neurospora crassa Database |publisher=Broad.mit.edu |date=April 9, 2014 |access-date=February 23, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080905171215/http://www.broad.mit.edu/annotation/fungi/neurospora_crassa_7/index.html |archive-date=September 5, 2008 }}</ref> and multiple relatives of ''[[Saccharomyces cerevisiae]]'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.yeastgenome.org/ |title=Saccharomyces Genome Database |publisher=Yeastgenome.org |date=February 18, 2015 |access-date=February 23, 2015}}</ref> one of the most studied [[yeast]]s.

Lander was the founding editor of the ''[[Annual Review of Genomics and Human Genetics]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XF8PAQAAMAAJ&dq=eric+lander+%22annual+review%22&pg=PA505|journal=Choice| title=Annual Reviews|publisher=Association of College and Research Libraries| year=2000}}</ref> He remained editor until 2004.

===After Human Genome Project===
Lander is the founding director of the [[Broad Institute]], a collaboration between MIT, Harvard, the Whitehead Institute, and affiliated hospitals.<ref name=":7">{{Cite news |date=17 July 2003 |title=Broad Institute created: Links Harvard, M.I.T., and others in interdisciplinary initiative in genomics and medicine |url=http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/07.17/11-broad.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070817095209/http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/07.17/11-broad.html |archive-date=17 August 2007 |work=Harvard Gazette}}</ref> Its goal is "to bring the power of genomics to bear on the understanding of disease and to accelerate the search for cures."<ref name=":7" /> In particular, Lander has discovered scientific facts in cell biology and molecular biology of cancer, as well as push [[precision medicine]] approaches.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Parsons |first=Lian |date=2021-01-15 |title=Broad Institute director tapped for White House role |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2021/01/broad-institute-director-tapped-for-white-house-role/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=Harvard Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref> He is often credited as among the drivers for the Broad Institute's meteoric rise during the 16 years he was a director.<ref name=":8" />

During the Obama presidency, Lander cochaired the Presidential Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eric Lander |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/node/26523 |access-date=2024-02-24 |website=The White House |language=en}}</ref>

=== Toast to James Watson ===
Lander toasted [[James Watson]] in 2018 for his 90th birthday, which caused controversy in the wake of Watson's widely criticized [[Race and intelligence|comments around intelligence and race.]]<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Begley |first=Sharon |date=2018-05-14 |title=As Twitter explodes, Eric Lander apologizes for toasting James Watson |url=https://www.statnews.com/2018/05/14/apology-eric-lander-james-watson/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=STAT |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |agency=[[500 Women Scientists]] |title=Eric Lander Is Not the Ideal Choice for Presidential Science Adviser |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/eric-lander-is-not-the-ideal-choice-for-presidential-science-adviser/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> Lander had included a brief aside in his toast stating that Watson was flawed, but still later apologized for his toast after significant outrage from academics on Twitter.<ref name=":4" /> [[Stat (website)|STAT News]] noted that other scientists had also similarly toasted Watson, but had not elicited similar outrage.<ref>{{Cite web | last1=Begley | first1=Sharon | last2=Joseph | first2=Andrew |date=May 17, 2018 |title=Scientific luminaries threw James Watson a birthday party weeks before Eric Lander's widely criticized toast |url=https://www.statnews.com/2018/05/17/james-watson-birthday-party-lander-toast/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=STAT |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== CRISPR-Cas 9 Controversy ===
Lander received criticism in the past for allegedly diminishing the accomplishments of [[Jennifer Doudna]] and [[Emmanuelle Charpentier]] after publishing "The Heroes of CRISPR" in [[Cell (journal)|Cell]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lander |first=Eric S. |date=January 2016 |title=The Heroes of CRISPR |journal=Cell |volume=164 |issue=1–2 |pages=18–28 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2015.12.041 |issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free |pmid=26771483 }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Achenbach |first=Joel |date=2021-10-27 |title=Eric Lander talks CRISPR and the infamous Nobel 'rule of three' |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2016/04/21/eric-lander-talks-crispr-and-the-infamous-nobel-rule-of-three/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Gravely |first=Alexis |title=Senators Question Science Nominee on Past Mistakes |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/05/04/nominee-lead-white-house-science-office-defends-himself-against-sexism-claims |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=Inside Higher Ed |language=en}}</ref> Some argued that his article was misogynistic for having [[Sexism in academia|removed women scientists]] from history.<ref name=":3" /> Of particular note, Lander was accused of a conflict of interest, as the Broad Institute had been competing with [[University of California, Berkeley|UC Berkeley]] for patent rights to commercialize CRISPR.<ref name=":2" /> Lander responded by suggesting he had not meant "to diminish anybody" and noted that science is collaborative by nature.<ref name=":2" /> Some argue that criticism was particularly harsh online by other academics and biologists due to previous resentment with Lander.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Begley |first=Sharon |date=2016-01-25 |title=Why Eric Lander morphed from science god to punching bag |url=https://www.statnews.com/2016/01/25/why-eric-lander-morphed/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=STAT |language=en-US}}</ref> During questioning for his role of [[Science Advisor to the President]], Lander admitted that he had made a mistake in understating the accomplishments of Doudna and Charpentier.<ref name=":3" />

===Science Advisor to the President===
In 2009, Lander was appointed by President Obama as co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), serving for the entire term (2009 to 2017).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/administration/advisory-boards/jobs-council/members/lander|title=Eric Lander The White House|access-date=2024-10-23}}</ref>

[[File:Eric Lander's swearing in as Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy.jpg|alt=Lander places hand on ancient text|thumb|Vice President Kamala Harris swears in Lander as director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, June 2021.]]

In January 2021, President-elect [[Joe Biden]] nominated Lander as [[Science Advisor to the President]] and announced that he would elevate the position to a [[Cabinet of the United States|Cabinet-level]] post.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|date=January 15, 2021|title=Biden picks geneticist as science adviser, elevates position to Cabinet|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/biden-picks-geneticist-as-science-adviser-elevates-position-to-cabinet|website=PBS NewsHour}}</ref> In January 2021, the organization "[[500 Women Scientists]]" published an editorial in ''[[Scientific American]]'' to consider naming someone else to the position, because he was well known within the scientific community for offending women.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/07/us/politics/eric-lander-resigns-white-house.html|title=Biden's Top Science Adviser Resigns After Acknowledging Demeaning Behavior|author=Katie Rogers |work=[[The New York Times]]|date=2022-02-08|access-date=2022-02-08}}</ref>
His nomination had been held up possibly due to requests for clarification about his having attended two gatherings where [[Jeffrey Epstein]], a wealthy large-scale donor to science who was also a convicted sex offender, was present.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/04/22/biden-top-scientist-met-jeffrey-epstein-confirmation-484159|title=Biden's top scientist met Jeffrey Epstein twice.It's now complicating his confirmation.|date=April 22, 2021|access-date=April 25, 2021|website=[[Politico]]|last1=Thompson|first1=Alex|last2=Meyer|first2=Theodoric|last3=Levine|first3=Marianne}}</ref> He was also questioned about accusations of sexism and his toast to James Watson.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-08 |title=Science Advisor Eric Lander Resigns in Disgrace |url=https://ww2.aip.org/fyi/2022/science-advisor-eric-lander-resigns-disgrace |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=AIP |language=en}}</ref> On April 29, a confirmation hearing was held in the [[United States Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation|Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Mervis|first=Jeffrey|date=April 29, 2021|title=Biden's nominee for science chief issues apology, defends character at confirmation hearing|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/biden-s-nominee-science-chief-issues-apology-defends-character-confirmation-hearing|access-date=May 1, 2021|website=Science}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Confirmation Hearing for White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Nominee|url=https://www.c-span.org/video/?511343-1/confirmation-hearing-white-house-office-science-technology-policy-director-nominee|access-date=May 1, 2021|website=[[C-SPAN]]|date=April 29, 2021}}</ref> On May 20, the committee voted to report favorably on the nomination, with five Republican senators voting against.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/05/20/biden-scientist-eric-lander-nomination-489798|title=Biden's top scientist gets OK from Senate committee|date=May 20, 2021|access-date=May 23, 2021|website=Politico|last1=Arciga|first1=Julia|last2=Din|first2=Benjamin}}</ref> On May 28, 2021, before a Memorial Day recess, his nomination was confirmed by voice vote by the full Senate. Lander was sworn in as director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) on June 2, 2021. He took his oath using a rare 1492 copy of the [[Pirkei Avot]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Tucker|first=Neely|date=June 4, 2021|title=The White House Scientist and the Ancient Jewish Book {{!}} Library of Congress Blog|url=https://blogs.loc.gov/loc/2021/06/the-white-house-scientist-and-the-ancient-jewish-book/|access-date=June 10, 2021|website=blogs.loc.gov}}</ref>

On February 7, 2022, ''[[Politico]]'' reported on a White House investigation in which fourteen current and former Office of Science and Technology Policy staffers accused Lander on February 4 of having bullied and demeaned his subordinates.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/02/07/eric-lander-white-house-investigation-00006077|title=Biden's top science adviser bullied and demeaned subordinates, according to White House investigation|date=February 7, 2022|access-date=February 7, 2022|last = Thompson|first = Alex|work = [[Politico]]}}</ref> Lander issued an apology to staff on February 4, his apology includes, "I am devastated that I caused hurt to past and present colleagues by the way in which I have spoken to them... I believe it is not possible to continue effectively in my role, and the work of this office is far too important to be hindered."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Zeke |title=White House: Top scientist resigns over treatment of staff |url=https://apnews.com/article/joe-biden-science-technology-health-jen-psaki-6b824f8341e4b1d54815c56a175e8d21 |website=APNews |publisher=AP |access-date=11 February 2022 |date=February 8, 2022}}</ref> He later resigned on February 7.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Thompson|first=Alex|title='I am deeply sorry for my conduct': Biden's top science adviser apologizes to staff|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/02/04/eric-lander-science-adviser-biden-apologize-00005988|access-date=2022-02-08|website=POLITICO|date=February 4, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Thompson|first=Alex|date=February 7, 2022|title=Biden's top science adviser, Eric Lander, resigns amid reports of bullying|work=[[Politico]]|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/02/07/eric-lander-resigns-00006545|access-date=February 7, 2022}}</ref> In the following month, ''Politico'' published an analysis of Lander's connections with [[Eric Schmidt]]. ''Politico'' documented the appearance of [[Conflict of interest|conflicts of interest]] related to Schmidt's financial support for many of the employees of the OSTP.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-28 |title=A Google billionaire's fingerprints are all over Biden's science office |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/03/28/google-billionaire-joe-biden-science-office-00020712 |access-date=2024-11-28 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref>

=== After resignation ===
Since 2023, Lander has returned to his tenured professor positions at MIT and Harvard as well as the Broad Institute as a Core Institute Member and Founding Director Emeritus.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Molteni |first=Megan |date=2023-05-12 |title=From fusion to retooling cancer trials, Eric Lander wants his new group to 'go after big problems' |url=https://www.statnews.com/2023/05/12/eric-lander-science-for-america/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=STAT |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite news |last=Lee |first=Stephanie M. |date=27 January 2023 |title=Eric Lander Left the White House Under a Cloud. Now He's Back at Work, and Not Everyone's Happy. |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/eric-lander-left-the-white-house-under-a-cloud-now-hes-back-at-work-and-not-everyones-happy |access-date=19 February 2024 |work=The Chronicle of Higher Education}}</ref> While some opinion pieces argued that "Eric Lander is getting [[Cancel culture|uncanceled]]",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goldberg |first=Carey |date=January 2023 |title=Eric Lander is getting uncanceled |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/01/27/opinion/eric-lander-is-getting-uncanceled/ |access-date=2024-02-20 |website=The Boston Globe |language=en-US}}</ref> ''[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]]'' noted that some staffers at the Broad expressed alarm at Lander's sudden return without further discussion from their leadership.<ref name=":9" /> In 2023, Lander started a non-profit called ''Science for America'' focused on "moonshot" ideas such as nuclear fusion or cancer research.<ref name=":6" />
====Fusion startup====
Lander became founding chief executive officer of [[Pacific Fusion]] in 2023 or 2024.<ref name=wired>{{cite news |last=Levy |first=Steven |title=A High-Profile Geneticist Is Launching a Fusion-Power Moonshot |url=https://www.wired.com/story/plaintext-pacific-fusion-eric-lander/ |work=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |date=25 October 2024}}</ref>

===Recognition and service===
In 1999, Lander received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=  https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref>

In 2004, Lander was named one of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine's [[Time 100|100 most influential people]] of our time for his work on the Human Genome Project. He has appeared in numerous [[PBS]] documentaries about genetics. He was ranked number 2 on the [[MIT150]] list of MIT's innovators and ideas.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Allis |first1=Sam |last2=Bray |first2=Hiawatha |last3=Helman |first3=Scott |url=https://archive.boston.com/news/education/higher/specials/mit150/mitlist/ |title=150 fascinating, fun, important, interesting, lifesaving, life-altering, bizarre and bold ways that MIT has made a difference |work=[[Boston.com]] |date=May 15, 2011 |access-date=February 9, 2021 }}</ref>

In December 2008, Lander and [[Harold E. Varmus]] were named co-chairs of the [[Obama administration]]'s [[Council of Advisors on Science and Technology]]. In 2012 he received the [[Dan David Prize]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.dandavidprize.org/laureates/2012/future-genome-research/eric-lander |title=Eric Lander |publisher=The Dan David Prize|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918143128/https://www.dandavidprize.org/laureates/2012/future-genome-research/eric-lander |archive-date=September 18, 2020 |access-date=January 15, 2021 }}</ref>

Lander is a member of the advisory board to the [[USA Science and Engineering Festival]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.usasciencefestival.org/about/advisors |title=USA Science and Engineering Festival – Advisors |publisher=Usasciencefestival.org |access-date=February 23, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100421005310/http://www.usasciencefestival.org/about/advisors/ |archive-date=April 21, 2010 }}</ref>

In 2013, Lander was awarded the first [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite news| url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2013/2/21/breakthrough-prize-awarded/ | title=Lander Awarded $3 Million |date= February 21, 2013 | first = Rachel J. | last = Sapire | access-date = May 26, 2020| newspaper =Harvard Crimson}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/20/science/new-3-million-prizes-awarded-to-11-in-life-sciences.html | title=At $3 Million, New Award Gives Medical Researchers a Dose of Celebrity| newspaper=The New York Times| date=February 20, 2013 | access-date = May 26, 2020 |last1=Overbye| first1=Dennis}}</ref> In 2016, [[Semantic Scholar]] AI program ranked him #1 on its list of most influential biomedical researchers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Who's the most influential biomedical scientist? Computer program guided by artificial intelligence says it knows|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/who-s-most-influential-biomedical-scientist-computer-program-guided-artificial|access-date=September 22, 2020|website=Science}}</ref>

In 2016, he received the Award for Excellence in Molecular Diagnostics from the [[Association for Molecular Pathology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.amp.org/membership/awards-grants-honors/amp-award-for-excellence-in-molecular-diagnostics/past-recipients/ |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=Association for Molecular Pathology |language=en}}</ref>

In 2017, Lander received an [[Honorary degree|''honoris causa'' doctorate]] from the [[Université catholique de Louvain]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://uclouvain.be/en/discover/events/eric-lander-mathematicien-et-geneticien.html|title=Eric Lander, mathematician and geneticist|website=UCLouvain|access-date=January 16, 2021|archive-date=March 16, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220316071034/https://uclouvain.be/en/discover/events/eric-lander-mathematicien-et-geneticien.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Also in 2017, he received the [[William Allan Award]] from the [[American Society of Human Genetics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ashg.org/awards/pastrecipients.shtml#allan|title=William Allan Award|publisher=ASHG|access-date=December 14, 2018|archive-date=August 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190804212043/http://www.ashg.org/awards/pastrecipients.shtml#allan}}</ref>

In 2019, he served on the Life Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]]. In 2020, [[Pope Francis]] appointed him a member of the [[Pontifical Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite press release | access-date = May 25, 2020 | date= May 25, 2020 | url = https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2020/05/25/200525b.html | title = Resignations and Assignments, 25.05.2020 | publisher = [[Holy See Press Office]] }}</ref> In 2021, Lander, who holds many patents, disclosed ownership of assets worth more than $45 million.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/bidens-wealthiest-cabinet-officials-zients-lander-rice-top-the-list-11616500809?mod=hp_featst_pos4|title = Biden's Wealthiest Cabinet Officials: Zients, Lander, Rice Top the List|newspaper = The Wall Street Journal|date = March 23, 2021}}</ref>
